newsitem.title: USA: Palestinian office in U.S. may be suspended.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian office in U.S. may be suspended.

text.p: The Palestinians' representative office in Washington may be forced to suspend operations in mid-August because its funding was not agreed when Congress adjourned on Friday for a month's holiday.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation office receives funds in the annual U.S. foreign aid bill which did not clear the House of Representatives.
As a result, authority to provide funds to the PLO through the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act expires on Aug. 12.

The lapse in funding was a procedural matter and not driven by the horror in Congress after this week's Jerusalem bomb attack, although the House did express frustration with the continued attacks in a separate vote.
The MEPFA, enacted in 1993 as part of the PLO's peace accord with Israel, was renewed in 1996 for 18 months. Congress cannot now act on a further extension until it returns on Sept. 2.
The lapse would affect the office and a small part of the overall U.S. payments to aid the Palestinians, which totals $500 million over the five years starting in 1994.
Said Hamad, the senior deputy chief representative at the PLO office, said the office would not actually close during the suspension and this was essentially a procedural problem.

Representative Nick Rahall, who sponsored extending the MEPFA, said the State Department was expected to have further talks on the issue in August with leaders of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the House International Relations Committee.

"Whatever negotiations produce between the leaders of committees between now and August 12 will probably be subject to approval by Congress," the West Virginia Democrat said. The negotiators could allow a temporary extension of the MEPFA until Congress acts, he said.
The MEPFA allows the president to waive many laws barring contacts and aid to the PLO, so long as he certifies they have lived up to the 1993 peace accord with Israel.
Separately, the House agreed late on Wednesday to suspend new aid to the PLO for three months after the fiscal 1998 appropriations bill takes effect.

Supporters of the suspension said it was a signal to the Palestinians that they must do more to stop terrorism. The vote occurred after Wednesday's bombing in a Jerusalem market that killed 15 people, including two suicide bombers.
The suspension was approved as an amendment offered by Republican Representative Jim Saxton of New Jersey to the pending foreign aid bill.
"It suspends direct aid to the Palestinian Authority...not money that is used legitimately to help upgrade living conditions for the Palestinian people," Saxton said.
He said the amount involved is about $10 million to $20 million of next year's $100 million U.S. aid to the Palestinian Authority, money used for its administration.
"What I did not want to do was just cut off aid and provide an excuse for Arafat to end the peace process," he said.
If the suspension is included over U.S. administration objections in the final bill sent to the president this fall, the aid would be available at the earliest on Jan. 1, 1998.

Rahall, who opposed the suspension of aid, called it "a political 'feel good' amendment of the kind that we do often in Congress," and said there would be room to make changes before the final bill is approved.
The Senate also approved, in its version of the foreign aid bill, some qualifications on aid to the Palestinian Authority after lawmakers expressed frustration with recent actions in the Middle East.
It voted to require the administration to send a detailed assessment of the Palestinian Authority's comliance with the 1993 peace accords, but would not suspend any funds.
